# Jobs

Background jobs in the app's own database, enqueued with its writes, retried with backoff, run in order per group, and checked at startup.

A job is work the app does after a request, or that a request should not wait for: mail an invoice, push a change to another system, recompute a report. Jobs live in the app's own Postgres database, in a schema named `jobs`, so a job can commit in the same transaction as the write that asks for it. The queue underneath is [pg-boss](https://github.com/timgit/pg-boss), pinned to one version; Protobase's own API in front of it is what the app uses.

A job is declared in `protobase.config.ts`, by its name, under `jobs`: what it does, its arguments and when it runs. What it does is the default export of `jobs/<name>.ts`, which Protobase finds by that path and loads the first time the job runs.

```ts title="protobase.config.ts"
import { defineConfig } from '@protobase/config'

export default defineConfig({
  // Each job's run is jobs/<name>.ts; the worker in `protobase dev` and `protobase serve` runs them.
  jobs: {
    'send-invoice': {
      description: 'Renders an invoice as a PDF and mails it to the customer.',
      arguments: { invoiceId: 'integer' },
      maxAttempts: 10, // then kept as failed, with its last error
      retryDelay: '30 seconds', // doubling with each retry, up to maxRetryDelay
    },
    'sync-customer': {
      description: 'Pushes the changed fields of a customer to the CRM.',
      arguments: { customerId: 'integer', fields: 'json' },
      ordered: true, // one at a time per customer, in the order the changes were made
    },
    'remind-overdue': {
      description: 'Mails a reminder for every invoice past its due date.',
      schedule: '0 7 * * *', // every morning at 7: one run per time, however many workers run
      timezone: 'Europe/Amsterdam',
    },
  },
  // hooks/queue-sent-invoice.ts
  writeHooks: ['queue-sent-invoice'],
})
```

```ts title="jobs/send-invoice.ts"
import { FatalJobError, type JobRun } from '@protobase/server'

export default (async ({ invoiceId }, { db }) => {
  const invoice = await db.selectFrom('sales.invoices').select(['id', 'status']).where('id', '=', invoiceId).executeTakeFirst()
  // Retrying will not bring it back: fail for good.
  if (!invoice) throw new FatalJobError(`Invoice ${invoiceId} is gone`)
  // ... render the PDF and mail it
}) satisfies JobRun<{ invoiceId: number }>
```

| Key of a job | |
| --- | --- |
| its name | Letters, digits, `_`, `-`, `.` and `/`; the file `jobs/<name>.ts` holds what it does. |
| `description` | What the job does, for the people who read the config. |
| `arguments` | Its arguments by name, each a [field type](data-config.md#field-types) such as `'integer'` or `'bigint'`, or the type with options: `{ type: 'enum', values: ['day', 'week'] }`, `{ type: 'text', min: 1 }`, `{ type: 'integer', optional: true }`, `{ type: 'decimal', precision: 8, scale: 2 }`. Each value is checked as a field of that type checks it, when the job is enqueued and again before it runs, and no other argument is taken. A payload refused at run time fails the job for good. The same is JSON in a `protobase.config.json`. |
| the default export of `jobs/<name>.ts` | `(payload, { db, job, signal, mail, sendNotification })`, typed with `JobRun<Payload>` from `@protobase/server`: the work. `db` is the app's pool: the enqueuer's transaction has committed by then. `job` holds its `id`, `name`, `attempt`, `maxAttempts` and `startedOn`, when this try took it. `signal` aborts when the try times out or the worker shuts down. `mail` sends mail, see [Mail](#mail). `sendNotification` sends a notification, see [Sending](notifications.md#sending); inside a transaction of `db`, a try that throws in it queues nothing. |
| `maxAttempts` | Tries before the job is kept as failed; default 10. |
| `retryDelay`, `maxRetryDelay` | The wait before the first retry, doubling with each one (with some jitter), and its ceiling; default `2s` and `1 hour`. Milliseconds or text such as `30 seconds`. |
| `timeout` | How long one try may run before it counts as failed; default `15 minutes`. |
| `concurrency` | Jobs of this name running at once in each worker process; default 1. |
| `longQueries` | Its queries through `db` may run up to 30 seconds instead of the database's own limit, for imports, backfills and large deletes; see [Long queries](../guides/api-functions.md#long-queries). A query stopped at its limit fails the try with an error that names the job. |
| `ordered` | Jobs run one at a time per group, in the order they were enqueued; see [Ordered groups](#ordered-groups). |
| `schedule`, `timezone` | Runs the job on a cron schedule, in a time zone (default the config's `timezone`, else `UTC`); see [Recurring jobs](#recurring-jobs). |

A job runs **at least once**: a worker that dies mid-job, or a try cut off by a shutdown, means it runs again. Write `run` so that running twice does no harm, for example by checking the state it is about to change.

## Enqueueing

```ts
import { enqueueJob } from '@protobase/server'

await enqueueJob(db, 'send-invoice', { invoiceId: 7 }, { delay: '5 minutes', key: 'invoice:7', priority: 10 })
```

`db` is the app's database, or the transaction of a write hook or an [API function](../guides/api-functions.md): there, the job commits with the caller's writes, or not at all. It returns the job's id. A write hook is named in the config's `writeHooks` and is the default export of `hooks/<name>.ts`:

```ts title="hooks/queue-sent-invoice.ts"
import { enqueueJob, type PipelineHook } from '@protobase/server'

// In the write's own transaction: the invoice and its job commit together or not at all.
export default (async (event, trx) => {
  if (event.resource.name !== 'invoices' || event.after?.status !== 'sent' || event.before?.status === 'sent') return
  const invoiceId = Number(event.after.id)
  await enqueueJob(trx, 'send-invoice', { invoiceId }, { key: `invoice:${invoiceId}` })
}) satisfies PipelineHook
```

| Option | |
| --- | --- |
| `runAt` or `delay` | When the job may run first: a `Date`, or milliseconds or text from now. Default now. |
| `priority` | Higher runs first; default 0. |
| `key` and `mode` | One waiting job per key: with `mode: 'dedupe'` (the default) an enqueue while one waits returns that one's id and leaves it as it is; with `mode: 'replace'` the waiting job takes this payload and these options. A job that is running does not count, so a change made while it runs gets a job of its own. |
| `group` | The group of an [ordered](#ordered-groups) job: required there, refused elsewhere. |

A job enqueued outside a transaction starts at once when this process runs its jobs. One enqueued in a transaction, or by another process, is picked up within the poll interval, 2 seconds.

Each worker takes one job per poll, so a queue that fills faster drains one job per worker every 2 seconds at first. Once the queue maintenance, about every minute, counts more jobs ready than the job's `concurrency`, a worker that found a job fetches the next one at once, until a fetch finds none: a backlog then drains as fast as its jobs run.

### From SQL

A trigger or a migration can enqueue in its own transaction:

```sql
select jobs.enqueue('send-invoice', '{"invoiceId": 7}');
select jobs.enqueue('send-invoice', '{"invoiceId": 7}', run_at => now() + interval '1 hour', key => 'invoice:7');
select jobs.enqueue('sync-customer', '{"customerId": 3, "fields": ["email"]}', group_key => 'customer:3');
```

`jobs.enqueue(job_name, payload, run_at, key, group_key, priority)` returns the job's id. A `key` dedupes as `mode: 'dedupe'` does. The job takes its retry settings from its definition, as the workers last saw it; a job no worker has started yet gets pg-boss's defaults until one does.

## Mail

`mail.send({ to, subject, text, html })` sends one message, with an optional HTML part beside the plain text, through the app's mail, the one that also sends password resets and sign-in codes: the mailer of `auth/mailer.ts` when the app has one, else the SMTP server of `PROTOBASE_SMTP_URL` and `PROTOBASE_MAIL_FROM` (see [Email](email.md#configuration)). An [email template](email.md#templates) sends through it with `template.send(to, data, mail)`. It rejects when the server refuses the message, so the try fails and is retried. Without either, `mail` is `undefined`: a job that must send fails for good with `FatalJobError`, and one that may skip mail leaves it out.

```ts
run: async ({ invoiceId }, { db, mail }) => {
  if (!mail) throw new FatalJobError('Mail is off: set PROTOBASE_SMTP_URL and PROTOBASE_MAIL_FROM')
  await mail.send({ to: 'customer@example.com', subject: `Invoice ${invoiceId}`, text: 'Your invoice is attached in the portal.' })
}
```

A message is sent once per try, so a try that sends and then fails sends again: record what was sent in the same run, and check it first.

## Failures

A try that throws is retried after its backoff, until `maxAttempts`. Then the job is kept as **failed** with its last error, for 7 days. `throw new FatalJobError('410 Gone')` fails it at once, without the attempts it has left.

A job that has waited 14 days past its start time without running is deleted.

While the database is read-only, as during a deploy's write freeze, a write in `run` fails with SQLSTATE `25006`: the try waits 5 seconds and runs `run` again, without using an attempt, until the database takes writes or the try times out.

## Ordered groups

With `ordered: true`, every enqueue names a `group`, and the jobs of one group run one at a time, in the order they were enqueued; different groups run side by side, up to `concurrency`. A job that is waiting for a retry, or has failed, holds back the rest of its group until it succeeds or is retried or deleted: that is what keeps the order. An ordered job takes no `key`: its group is how pg-boss finds its jobs.

Turning `ordered` on or off for a job whose queue exists stops startup: let its jobs finish or delete them, then drop the queue with `select jobs.delete_queue('<name>')`.

## Recurring jobs

`schedule: '0 7 * * *'` runs a job on that cron schedule, with no payload; a seconds field may come first (`*/30 * * * * *`). `timezone` reads it in a zone such as `Europe/Amsterdam`, so 07:00 stays 07:00 across daylight saving time.

Each run is a job of its own, enqueued ahead for its time by the workers: its id is made from the job's name and the time, so however many workers enqueue a run, it is one job and runs once. As a run starts, the next one is enqueued. A run that came due while no worker ran, as when the app slept or was deployed, runs once as soon as one does; the times missed after it are skipped. Changing the schedule drops the waiting run that is no longer one of its times, and a job that loses its schedule, or is removed, loses its waiting run.

Because the next run waits in the database like any delayed job, [`jobs.next_due()`](#hosts-that-sleep) sees it, and a host that wakes the app for due jobs wakes it for its recurring jobs too. That is why Protobase does not use pg-boss's own scheduler, which keeps no next run in the database and works the time out in a running process.

## Failed jobs page

With jobs, the admin app has a **Failed jobs** page, for admins only: each job that used up its attempts or failed for good, with its payload and last error. **Retry** gives a job one more attempt, from now, and **Delete** removes it. It reads the `jobs.failed` view, which a project's SQL can query too.

## Where jobs run

- **`protobase dev`** runs them in its process. An edited job runs its new code from the next job on.
- **`protobase serve`** runs them in its process, beside the API, unless `PROTOBASE_JOBS=false`; it enqueues them either way. On SIGTERM it stops taking jobs and gives running ones 30 seconds to finish. A job still running then is failed, to be retried.
- **[`protobase worker <bundle>`](cli.md#worker)** runs the same jobs from the same bundle in a process of its own, with the same shutdown, for a `serve` with `PROTOBASE_JOBS=false`.
- Each worker checks every job name for due jobs every 2 seconds: one indexed query per job name and interval. Once a minute, one of the workers also counts the queues and retries the jobs whose worker died (their `timeout` passed); once a day it deletes completed and failed jobs older than 7 days.

### Hosts that sleep

A host that stops an idle app needs to know when a job is due, and to have it run:

- `select jobs.next_due()` answers when the next job is due, or `null` when none waits: a waiting job's start time, a recurring job's next run, or the timeout of a job that was running when the app stopped. It is one read-only statement, through any pooler.
- `POST /api/jobs/drain?seconds=25` runs the due jobs until none is due or running, or the seconds have passed, and answers `{ "drained": true, "remaining": 0, "nextDue": "2026-10-12T05:00:00.000Z" }`. It takes the operator's token, `PROTOBASE_JOBS_DRAIN_TOKEN`, as a bearer token; without that variable there is no such endpoint. A process with `PROTOBASE_JOBS=false` answers `409`.

## The `jobs` schema

The schema is pg-boss's tables at its pinned schema version, plus Protobase's `jobs.enqueue`, `jobs.next_due` and `jobs.failed`. It is created and upgraded like the [auth schema](auth.md#migrations), by the project's migrations:

```sh
bun run protobase migration   # writes db/migrations/NNN_jobs.sql when the jobs schema is missing or behind
bun run db:migrate
```

[`protobase migration`](cli.md#migration) writes what the database lacks, taken from pg-boss's own construction and migration plans for the pinned version, without their `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` and with any `CONCURRENTLY` index build made a plain one, so the file runs in the project's migration transaction. The server never creates or migrates it: `protobase dev` and `protobase serve` read its version at startup and refuse to start while it is missing or behind, naming the command. A database whose jobs schema is newer than the running Protobase is refused too.

pg-boss runs here without what needs a session of its own: no `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` (a job enqueued in the same process wakes its worker directly, the rest is polled), only transaction-scoped advisory locks, unnamed prepared statements, no index rebuilds and no instance registry. It works through PgBouncer in transaction mode and on PGlite, over the app's own connection pool.
